question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{-5/9}$ and that ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$ Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{5}{9}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-5/9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-5/9+1}}{(-\frac{5}{9}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4/9}}{(\frac{4}{9})}+C \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{x}^{4/9}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: What is the antiderivative of $\frac{1}{{x}^{8}}?$ Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{8}}={x}^{-8}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-8$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{8}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{-8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-8+1}}{-8+1}+C \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{-7}}{7}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{7{x}^{7}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
